title: The technologies worth knowing by name
dek: Ten technologies interviewers expect you to recognise: what each is for, when to reach for it, a number to remember, and the catch. Each points to its full article in Components.

head: If you need
Reach for
rows: The record of truth, with transactions
Fast reads of hot data, counters, rankings
Events many services react to, or replay
A search box with words, typos and ranking
Huge write rates, queries known in advance
Key lookups at any scale, nothing to run
A process of many steps that must finish
One front door: auth, limits, routing
body.label: Which tool for which need

body.x: Redis
An in-memory store of data structures: strings, hashes, sorted sets, streams.

items: Reach for it for: A cache, counters, rate limits, leaderboards (sorted sets), short-lived locks, sessions.
A number to remember: Around a lakh simple operations a second per node; a command takes well under a millisecond.
The catch: It lives in memory: size it, and don't rely on it as the only copy of data you can't lose.
Read: 'Redis' in Components.

body.x: Elasticsearch
A search engine built on an inverted index: for every word, the documents that contain it.

items: Reach for it for: A search box: words, typos, ranking, filters, places near the user.
A number to remember: New documents become searchable after about a second; aim for shards of 10 to 50 GB.
The catch: Not the source of truth: keep the database as the record and feed the index from it.
Read: 'Elasticsearch' in Components.

body.x: Kafka
A durable, partitioned log of events that many services read at their own pace.

items: Reach for it for: Events several services react to, very high write rates, keeping order per key, replaying history.
A number to remember: One partition takes tens of MB a second; events are kept 7 days by default.
The catch: Order holds only within a partition; consumers must cope with seeing an event twice.
Read: 'Kafka in practice' in Components.

body.x: Temporal
A workflow engine that runs ordinary code as a process that survives crashes, deploys and long waits.

items: Reach for it for: Multi-step processes across services with retries, timeouts and waits of hours or days: orders, payouts, refunds.
A number to remember: A step costs tens of milliseconds; waiting a day is just a stored timer.
The catch: Workflow code must be deterministic; it is another system to run, so use it when a state machine in your database would be painful.
Read: 'Temporal' in Components.

body.x: API gateway
One front door for many services: ends HTTPS, checks who is calling, rate-limits and routes.

items: Reach for it for: Several services, outside partners or apps, per-client limits.
A number to remember: Managed gateways cost about $1 to $3.50 per million requests; some cut requests off at about 30 seconds.
The catch: It adds a few milliseconds and, at high traffic, a real bill; uploads and long work go around it.
Read: 'API gateways' in Components.

body.x: Cassandra
A wide-column database with no leader: every node takes reads and writes, data is copied around a ring.

items: Reach for it for: Very high write rates, data spread across regions, queries known in advance (one table per query).
A number to remember: Replication factor 3 is usual; keep a partition under about 100 MB.
The catch: No joins and no ad-hoc queries; deletes leave tombstones that slow reads.
Read: 'Cassandra' in Components.

body.x: DynamoDB
A managed key-value and document store: no servers to size, patch or fail over.

items: Reach for it for: Key lookups at any scale with little to run, when every query can use a key you designed in advance.
A number to remember: One partition takes about 1,000 writes and 3,000 reads a second; an item is at most 400 KB.
The catch: Queries outside your keys need a full scan or a new index; a hot partition key hits its limit early.
Read: 'DynamoDB' in Components.

body.x: PostgreSQL
The default relational database: transactions, SQL, rich indexes, JSON and geospatial queries.

items: Reach for it for: Most designs, as the place where the truth lives, until a number says otherwise.
A number to remember: One primary takes thousands of writes and tens of thousands of reads a second on good hardware.
The catch: Writes go through one primary; past that you shard, by hand or with a tool such as Citus.
Read: 'PostgreSQL' in Components.

body.x: Flink
A stream processor: answers computed as events arrive, with state per key and exactly-once recovery.

items: Reach for it for: Counts per minute, live fraud checks, live ETAs: anything that must be answered while the data is still flowing.
A number to remember: End-to-end latency of milliseconds to seconds; state up to terabytes on local disk.
The catch: It's a cluster to run: for simple counting, a consumer writing to Redis may be enough.
Read: 'Flink' in Components.

body.x: ZooKeeper
A small, consistent tree of data that a cluster agrees on, with watches and nodes that vanish when their owner dies.

items: Reach for it for: Leader election, locks, configuration and membership for other systems.
A number to remember: An ensemble of 3 survives one failure, 5 survives two; writes run at thousands a second.
The catch: For coordination only, never for application data; etcd and Consul do the same job.
Read: 'ZooKeeper' in Components.
